text.en: A cell cannot burn glucose directly for energy. It first converts the energy into ATP, the cell's currency, and the mitochondrion is the mint.

Mitochondria are double-membrane organelles that make ATP, so they are called the power house of the cell.
The outer membrane is smooth and freely permeable; the inner membrane is folded into cristae and carries oxysomes (F1 particles) that make ATP.
The matrix contains enzymes for the Krebs cycle, 70S ribosomes, tRNA and mitochondrial DNA.
External respiration is gas exchange with the environment; cellular respiration is the biochemical oxidation of food to release energy.
Aerobic respiration oxidises glucose completely with oxygen: C6H12O6 + 6O2 gives 6CO2 + 6H2O + ATP.
Stage 1, glycolysis, occurs in the cytoplasm and splits one glucose (6C) into two pyruvic acid (3C) molecules; it is common to aerobic and anaerobic respiration.
Stage 2, the Krebs or TCA cycle, occurs in the mitochondrial matrix and oxidises pyruvic acid to carbon dioxide.
Stage 3, the electron transport chain on the inner membrane, oxidises NADH and FADH2; the electrons release energy to make ATP (oxidative phosphorylation) and oxygen is the final electron acceptor, forming water.
Anaerobic respiration occurs without oxygen: yeast gives ethanol and carbon dioxide (ethanol fermentation) and bacteria give lactic acid.
Respiratory quotient RQ = volume of CO2 liberated divided by volume of O2 consumed.

problem.en: Calculate the RQ when 6 volumes of CO2 are released while 6 volumes of O2 are consumed.

text.en: RQ = volume of CO2 liberated / volume of O2 consumed.
RQ = 1, which is typical for oxidation of carbohydrates such as glucose.
